title: Week 1 · Lesson 2: Cellular Adaptation & Inflammation — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 1 — Lesson 2: Cellular Adaptation & Inflammation

FNP-level goal: Recognize when a cellular response is an adaptation, when it signals chronic disease risk, and when an inflammatory presentation requires urgent escalation rather than routine outpatient follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, and metaplasia by mechanism and clinical pattern.
  • Distinguish acute from chronic inflammation and relate each to expected cells, mediators, and outcomes.
  • Use redness, warmth, edema, pain, and fever as physiologic clues—not diagnoses.
  • Build a safe differential for a red, painful, swollen extremity.
  • Recognize red flags for necrotizing soft-tissue infection and systemic illness.

Part 1 — Adaptation Before Injury

Cells respond to changes in workload, nutrients, hormones, oxygen delivery, and environmental stress. If the demand is manageable, cells may adapt and maintain function. If stress persists or exceeds adaptive capacity, injury develops.

Normal cell → adaptation → injury → recovery or irreversible injury → cell death.

The FNP question is: What chronic driver is the tissue responding to? The answer may be hypertension, hormones, disuse, denervation, ischemia, tobacco exposure, reflux, chronic infection, or inflammation.

Part 2 — Hypertrophy: More Work Per Cell

Hypertrophy = increased cell size. It is important in tissues with limited proliferative capacity, including myocardium.

Chronic hypertension → afterload ↑ → cardiomyocyte workload ↑ → LV hypertrophy.

Initially, hypertrophy helps generate force. Long term, a thick ventricle has increased oxygen demand and impaired relaxation: LVH → stiffness → diastolic dysfunction → elevated filling pressure → dyspnea/HFpEF risk.

FNP reasoning: LVH is not merely an ECG or echo label. It should trigger attention to blood-pressure control, symptoms, kidney disease, ischemic risk, and adherence.

Part 3 — Hyperplasia: More Cells

Hyperplasia = increased number of cells in tissue capable of cell division. It can be physiologic or pathologic.

Examples include hormone-responsive endometrium and compensatory growth in selected tissues. Persistent unopposed estrogen can drive endometrial hyperplasia.

Clinical reasoning: abnormal uterine bleeding plus prolonged unopposed-estrogen exposure, obesity, chronic anovulation, or postmenopausal status should not be reduced to “hormonal bleeding.” The question is whether endometrial pathology needs timely evaluation.

Hyperplasia is not cancer, but persistent abnormal proliferative signaling can raise future dysplasia/malignancy risk in the appropriate tissue and context.

Part 4 — Atrophy: Less Work, Less Mass

Atrophy = decreased cell size and functional capacity; cell number can also decrease depending on cause and tissue.

Causes include decreased workload, denervation, poor nutrition, reduced blood supply, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure, and aging.

Disuse → reduced workload → protein synthesis ↓ and protein breakdown ↑ → muscle atrophy.

FNP reasoning: progressive weakness or wasting requires a cause-directed assessment. Consider immobilization, neurologic deficit, inadequate nutrition, endocrine disease, malignancy, chronic organ disease, medication effects, and functional safety—not only exercise advice.

Part 5 — Metaplasia: A Different Mature Cell Type

Metaplasia = reversible replacement of one mature differentiated cell type by another mature cell type better suited to a chronic stress.

In smoking-related airway injury, normal ciliated epithelium can be replaced by squamous epithelium. The new cells may better tolerate irritation, but mucociliary clearance is impaired. In chronic reflux, Barrett esophagus is a clinically important metaplastic change.

Metaplasia is not cancer. However, persistence of the injurious stimulus can progress toward dysplasia in some settings. Removing the driver and arranging appropriate surveillance are more useful than alarmist labeling.

Part 6 — Inflammation Is a Response, Not a Diagnosis

Inflammation aims to eliminate injury, clear damaged tissue, and begin repair. It can be caused by infection, ischemia, trauma, toxins, crystals, autoimmunity, and other sterile injury.

Inflammation ≠ infection. A swollen red joint may be septic arthritis, crystal disease, inflammatory arthritis, or trauma. A warm red leg may be cellulitis, DVT, venous stasis dermatitis, contact dermatitis, or a necrotizing infection.

Part 7 — Acute Inflammation

Acute inflammation is rapid and commonly features vascular changes plus neutrophil recruitment.

Vasodilation → local blood flow ↑ → redness and warmth.

Vascular permeability ↑ → protein-rich fluid enters tissue → edema.

Mediators also sensitize nociceptors and tissue pressure rises, contributing to pain and loss of function.

The recruitment sequence is a useful mental model: margination → rolling → adhesion → diapedesis → chemotaxis. Neutrophils kill pathogens and clear debris, but excessive enzymes and ROS can injure host tissue.

Part 8 — Chronic Inflammation

Chronic inflammation reflects persistent injury, impaired resolution, or both. Macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells commonly participate; tissue destruction and repair occur together.

Persistent stimulus → macrophage/lymphocyte activation → cytokines + tissue injury + fibroblast activation → remodeling/fibrosis.

Examples include autoimmune disease, persistent infection, chronic irritant exposure, atherosclerosis, and some metabolic disease. Chronic inflammation can therefore contribute to structural damage even when symptoms fluctuate.

Part 9 — Cytokines, Acute-Phase Response, and Fever

TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are major inflammatory signaling mediators. They support leukocyte recruitment and systemic responses. IL-6 contributes to hepatic acute-phase protein production; markers such as CRP can support an inflammatory pattern but cannot independently identify the cause.

Inflammatory signaling → PGE2 in the hypothalamus → temperature set point ↑ → fever.

Fever is a physiologic clue. FNP reasoning requires severity assessment, exposure history, source-directed examination, host risk factors, and disposition—not automatic antibiotic prescribing.

Part 10 — FNP Differential: Red, Warm, Swollen Leg

Do not stop at “cellulitis.” Use location, symmetry, onset, fever, skin findings, trauma, edema, venous history, thrombotic risk, diabetes/immunosuppression, and pain severity.

  • Cellulitis/abscess: infection pattern; look for portal of entry, fluctuance, purulence, fever, and progression.
  • DVT: unilateral swelling/pain may occur; assess thrombotic risk and use an appropriate diagnostic pathway.
  • Venous stasis dermatitis: commonly chronic and often bilateral, with edema and skin change.
  • Contact dermatitis: exposure pattern, pruritus, and sharply defined distribution can help.
  • Necrotizing soft-tissue infection: uncommon but time-critical.

Part 11 — Do Not Miss: Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection

Red flags include pain out of proportion, rapidly progressive symptoms, systemic toxicity, hypotension, bullae, skin necrosis/discoloration, crepitus, anesthesia, or severe illness in an immunocompromised patient.

If clinical suspicion is high, this is an emergency. Imaging can assist in some uncertain cases but must not delay urgent surgical evaluation when a necrotizing infection is suspected.

Part 12 — Board-Style Case 1

A 68-year-old with long-standing hypertension has exertional dyspnea and echo evidence of concentric LVH.

Mechanism: chronic afterload ↑ → cardiomyocyte hypertrophy → ventricular stiffness → impaired relaxation and higher filling pressures.

FNP next questions: blood-pressure trend, adherence, renal function, ischemic symptoms, signs of HF, and whether symptoms require further cardiovascular evaluation.

Part 13 — Board-Style Case 2

A patient has a painful, rapidly enlarging erythematous thigh, fever, tachycardia, and pain far greater than expected from the initial skin appearance.

Do not call this uncomplicated cellulitis and schedule review. The pattern raises concern for a necrotizing soft-tissue process: arrange emergency evaluation and urgent escalation.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Hypertrophy: bigger cells; chronic pressure/workload.

Hyperplasia: more cells; hormonal or compensatory signaling.

Atrophy: less cell mass/function; disuse, denervation, poor nutrition, ischemia, or endocrine loss.

Metaplasia: a different mature cell type; adaptation to chronic stress, with context-specific surveillance implications.

Acute inflammation: fast, vascular change, often neutrophil-predominant.

Chronic inflammation: persistent stimulus, macrophages/lymphocytes, injury plus repair/fibrosis.

FNP decision: name the inflammatory pattern, find the cause, rule out time-sensitive alternatives, and escalate based on stability and red flags.
